SEC12A-01.note: Semicolon joins two independent clauses with the participial phrase fronting the second. B comma splice, D run-on. C is grammatical-looking but strands the participle on 'seismometers' (dangling) and moves the causal phrase away from the collapse; struck on sense by most. PHASE 2: agree; explanation's dangling-modifier argument for C is correct (and 'its' cannot refer to seismometers).

SEC12A-02.note: Dash-opened appositive must close with a dash before the main verb 'remains'. Classic SAT pattern; the long appositive hides the opening dash. PHASE 2: key and explanation agree with my cold solve; explanation is sound.

SEC12A-03.note: Comma closes the comma-opened relative clause; 'also illustrated' is the main verb. D ('and also') folds the verb into the relative clause, leaving no main verb; B mismatches comma/dash (inner dashes are a lure); A semicolon leaves a fragment. PHASE 2: key and explanation agree with my cold solve; explanation is sound.

SEC12A-04.note: Colon introduces the semicolon-separated list of the 'several independent records'. A and B leave the list as a fragment; C comma before a semicolon list is wrong. PHASE 2: key and explanation agree with my cold solve; explanation is sound.

SEC12A-05.note: 'however' interrupts a single clause (fronted prepositional phrase + main clause), so paired commas. B semicolon makes the long prepositional phrase a fragment - the real lure. C and D drop one of the pair; strikeable on sight. PHASE 2: key and explanation agree with my cold solve; explanation is sound.

SEC12A-06.note: Second clause has a noun-clause subject ('whether ... remained disputed'), so it is independent: semicolon. A comma splice, C run-on, D 'as to whether' removes the subject of 'remained'. PHASE 2: key and explanation agree with my cold solve; explanation is sound.

SEC12A-07.note: 'with remarkably little loss' is the only option yielding a grammatical sentence; B and D produce verbless fragments, A leaves a stranded noun phrase. C is the odd-one-out (only option with a word instead of a mark). PHASE 2: key correct; item is easy and C is the only option that is a word rather than a mark, an odd-one-out tell.

SEC12B-01.note: Shifted object: 'makes visible [to anyone with a microscope] the filaments' - no punctuation between verb complement and object. A (comma) is the strong lure because the long phrase feels like it needs a pause; C fragment, B 'and' nonsense. PHASE 2: key and explanation agree with my cold solve; explanation is sound.

SEC12B-02.note: Two independent clauses joined by 'but' need the comma before it; the because-clause is introductory to the second clause and closes at 'note,'. B is a comma splice (because-clause then new clause). D omits the comma before 'but' with two long clauses - nonstandard on SAT but some style guides tolerate omission; A puts the comma after 'but' (permissible) but still lacks the one before it. PHASE 2: agree; explanation correctly rejects A (comma after 'but' does not replace the one before it). Best item in the batch.

SEC12B-03.note: Colon introduces the explanation of 'something'. A comma splice, C run-on, D 'which the mapmaker had sketched the shoreline' is ungrammatical on sight. PHASE 2: key and explanation agree with my cold solve; explanation is sound.

SEC12B-04.note: Sentence-final summative appositive ('a pattern that ...') takes a dash. B and C leave the appositive as a fragment; D has no boundary at all. PHASE 2: key and explanation agree with my cold solve; explanation is sound.

SEC12B-05.note: 'however' starts a new independent clause: semicolon before, comma after. A comma splice is the lure; B and C drop required punctuation. PHASE 2: key and explanation agree with my cold solve; explanation is sound.

SEC12B-06.note: Comma closes the comma-opened relative clause(s) before the main verb 'shares'. A dash mismatches the opening comma; B semicolon splits subject from verb; D omits the closing comma. PHASE 2: key and explanation agree with my cold solve; explanation is sound.

SEC12B-07.convention: Negative-adverbial inversion ('only after X did Y begin') is grammatical inside a subordinate clause, so 'guilds, although only after ... did western European mills begin' conforms; its fault is that 'although' is not concessive here, which is a logic/transition criterion, not SEC.
SEC12B-07.note: Inverted 'Only after ... did mills begin' is an independent clause, so it needs a sentence boundary: B. A comma splice, C run-on. D survives grammatically and fails only on the meaning of 'although'. PHASE 2: key B is correct and best, but the explanation's last sentence is false: negative inversion IS possible in an 'although' clause ('although only rarely did they...' is grammatical; peripheral adverbial clauses allow it). D is therefore grammatical and fails only on the non-concessive logic of 'although'. Repair D (e.g. an option that is ungrammatical on structure) and fix the explanation before shipping.
